R001_stomachdrops.caption:
Dealing with a toxic boss doesn't stop when you clock out.

Your boss's name lights up your phone at 9:47 p.m. and your chest tightens before you've even read the message. You replay the meeting on the drive home. You check your email one more time before bed, just in case.

That reaction isn't you being dramatic. When work keeps putting you on guard, your body learns to stay ready. Noticing it is the first step to taking your evenings back.

Send this to the coworker who checks their phone the same way.

R002_reliable.caption:
Burnout at work doesn't always come from doing too much. Sometimes it comes from being too good at it.

You finish early, so you get the extra project. You never complain, so you get the weekend coverage. You're dependable, so your workload keeps growing while the recognition stays the same.

Being reliable is a strength. It isn't permission for unlimited work. "I can take this on if the other project moves to next week" is a boundary, not a lack of commitment.

Which part of this happens most at your workplace? Follow @unspokenatwork1 so this finds you again the next time the list gets longer.

C001_document.caption:
Dealing with a bad boss is exhausting, and trying to remember every incident makes it worse.

When something happens, whether it's a comment in front of the team, a deadline that suddenly changed, or a message that crossed a line, write it down the same day. Date, time, place, the exact words, and who was there. Keep it calm and factual, with no labels and no guessing at motives.

Store your notes somewhere personal that you control, and keep any related emails or messages you're allowed to keep. If things escalate, a clear record helps HR or an employment professional understand what happened. This is general information, not legal advice.

Save this for the day you need it, and follow @unspokenatwork1 so it finds you again when you do.

R003_quickchat.caption:
Workplace anxiety has a very specific sound: a vague meeting invite from your boss with no description.

Friday, 4:55 PM. "Quick chat." Suddenly you're replaying every email from the week, and the weekend feels gone before it starts.

You're allowed to ask what it's about. "Happy to! What's it about, so I can come prepared?" is calm, professional, and gives you something solid instead of a spiral. Then do one thing tonight that's just for you.
